content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies a generative model to model temporal graphs that have temporally changing nodes/edges and their features. The authors claim that the proposed method learns the data distribution well and generates the robust and accurate synthetic data for continuous-time dynamic graphs. In addition, the proposed method shows good performance in future edge prediction in the inductive setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The authors achieved comparable performance in future edge prediction.
	 
Weaknesses:
* The authors did not compare their method with any other generative models for temporal graphs. Even if the regime is not extensively explored, there are tons of generative models for time-series data. Authors must compare their methods with a simple adoption of such generative models in this context. 
* The main contribution is weak. This paper does not have any novel component which addresses technical challenges. Fitting the generative model to the data is not sufficient to be considered as a significant contribution.
* More experimental results are needed with stronger and more recent baselines. The TGN-attn is 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Clarity: Writing definitely needs to be improved. The motivation and technical challenges are not clear. 
* Quality: it shows great performance on the benchmark datasets with almost perfect AP. It is questionable. It might be overfitting to the benchmark datasets. The lack of technical contributions and analyses makes these experimental results less convincing.
* Novelty: no significant contribution
* Reproducibility: the proposed model has TGN as an encoder and some deep probabilistic models equipped with GMM. It is not clear whether this model is stably optimizable.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper does not have sufficient technical contributions. Although the experimental results indicate that the proposed model achieved perfect-like performance, baselines are not recent methods, and analyses are not comprehensive. It seems that benchmark datasets are saturated as well. The authors might consider other more challenging datasets.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a generative framework for Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs (CTDG) based on an encoder for temporal node embeddings and a decoder for learning a probabilistic network model. The results show the generalizable capabilities of the proposed generative model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. The paper is well motivated and the need for generative approaches for CTDGs is well justified 
2. The paper is easy to read and follow.  
3. The experiments and ablation are detailed lend confidence in the author’s claims.  
4. The encoder and decoder module designs naturally fit the generative CTDG regime 
5. Why is ROLAND model not used in the encoder even though it is mentioned and an essential part of prior literature? 
6. The authors do not provide statistical significance for the difference in real and synthetic distributions 
7. An example figure can help illustrate the problem setting well. 
8. There is an important and recent paper [1] which is not considered in this paper.  
[1] INDUCTIVE REPRESENTATION LEARNING IN TEMPORAL NETWORKS VIA CAUSAL ANONYMOUS WALKS
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written and somewhat novel.  
Minor comments and typos about the writing: 
1. “manifolds(Wu et al., 2020a;b)” -> “manifolds (WU et al.,”: Page 1, Introduction 
2. “..embeddings to cereate a deep…” -> “...embeddings to create a deep…”: Page 2, Contributions 
3. “..using based on this memory.” -> “based on this memory”, Page 2, Representation learning for dynamic graphs 
4. “..by recurrently update their state” -> “by recurrently updating their state”: Page 2, Representation learning for dynamic graphs 
5. “These include Zeno et al. (2021) which graph” -> “Zeno et al. (2021) which uses”: Page 3, Generative models for graph data 
6. “For distrubtions at…” -> “For distributions at..”: Page 7, Graph Generation

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a generative model is proposed for learning the temporal graphs. TGN is adopted as the encoder of the framework. The decoder is used to learning the distribution of a temporal interaction data. The proposed model is tested on both the representation learning tasks and the graph generation tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1.	Well-designed experiments in validating the proposed models.
2.	This paper deals a very promising and interesting problem.

Weakness:
1.	This paper is not well written. No problem formulation is clearly provided, and no notations are given. Please see details in the following summary of the review.
2.	The contribution and novelty of this paper is limited. The proposed model is about a combination of existing graph encoder and decoder. The contribution is not clear stated. 
3.	The discussion and comparison with some existing temporal graph generation models is missing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1.	This paper is easy to reproduce given the code provided. 
2.	The novelty is limited since the proposed model is a combination of existing works (e.g.TGN).
3.	The paper needs more clarity on the problem formulation, notations, and typical mathematical formulations in describing the method, instead of obscure “plain text”.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The major concern of this paper is the limited contribution and novelty, as well as the low quality of paper writing. Followings are the detailed comments or confusing pints that needs clarifications from authors.
1. It is unclear what is the difference between CTDG and DTDG. The author claims that DTGTs are a set of snapshots of graphs at different time points, while the proposed method for CTDG also have the element of “t” as the time point. I have doubts towards the rationality of this classification. It would be better if more detailed description and illustrative real-world examples given on these two categories respectively. It is not clear whether CTDG and DTDG are different from problem-level or technique-level, namely, are they solving the different problem or solving the same problem from different ways?

2. The authors claims they are the first to deal with generative models for temporal graph. However, there are some existing generative models for temporal graphs, such as [1-3]. More discussions and even comparison experiments need to be added. 
[1] Zhang, L. 2019. STGGAN: Spatial-temporal graph generation. In Proceedings of the 27th ACM SIGSPATIAL International Conference on Advances in Geographic Information Systems, 608–609.
[2] Zhang, L.; Zhao, L.; Qin, S.; and Pfoser, D. 2020. TG-GAN:Deep Generative Models for Continuously-time Temporal Graph Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2005.08323
[3] Du Y, Guo X, Cao H, Ye Y, Zhao L. Disentangled Spatiotemporal Graph Generative Models. AAAI 2022.

3.	It is unclear how the proposed model can model the time dependency of the temporal graphs. In Figure 1, only one temporal interaction data is inputted into the model. Thus, how the prediction is based on the history data? 

4.	There is no formal problem formulation and clear notations before introducing the methodology. It is hard for readers to know the meaning of each symbol and the objective of the problem. For example, what is “v” refers to? And what is the relationship between the “interaction” and “edge”?

5.	The encoder learns the latent embeddings “z” of the input, but the decoder seems not to be dependent on “z” based on Section 3.2. I assume the probability learnt by the decoder is incorrect. For decoder, it should p(dst|z) and for the overall model, it can be p(dst|src). I suggest a clarification of what distribution is modeled by encoder and decoder respectively.

6.	Some typos, like “said embeddings to”.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response Statement from Authors
content.comment:
We would like to thank all the reviewers for taking the time to leave detailed and honest feedback on our work. We are happy to see that the reviewers believe that the approach taken is promising. However, we also acknowledge that more work has to be done in areas such as comparison to state-of-the-art architectures for the link prediction task and adaptation of models from the generative DTDG domain for use as baselines.

As such, we are withdrawing our paper from consideration and will work on incorporating these improvements in a future submission.

Sincerely,

The Paper5771 Authors
